title: Puppets & Storytelling
strapline: A sock, a stick and a different voice — suddenly even the quietest child has a lot to say.
intent: Children retell known stories and invent their own, building narrative structure — beginning, middle, end — through their hands.
Children experiment with voice: volume, pitch, character voices and the rhythm of dialogue.
Children who find talking hard borrow a puppet's confidence — the puppet speaks, so they can too.
Children negotiate shared storylines: who is the wolf, what happens next, whose turn on the story stage.
Children explore feelings safely at one remove — a sad puppet can be comforted, a cross puppet can be calmed.
implementation: Match puppets to your core books first — a retell only takes off when children already own the story.
Model puppet talk yourself: give it a voice, make it whisper to you, let it get things charmingly wrong so children correct it.
Use a shy puppet at group time to draw out quiet children — many will talk to a puppet long before they talk to the group.
Step back once a story starts; narrate from the side ('and THEN what did the troll do?') rather than taking the strings.
Offer open-ended story-makers too — pegs, felt, wooden spoons, small-world figures — so children can build the character they need.
Let the puppet have feelings that need naming: 'Monkey looks worried today — what could we do?'
Keep a simple story stage or table-top screen available daily, not just as a one-off provocation.
key_questions: What kind of voice does this character have?
What happens next in your story?
How is the puppet feeling — how can you tell?
What could we use to make the giant?
How will your story end — and could it end a different way?

impact.text: Children retell familiar stories loosely with puppets and props, holding the shape of the tale.
Children narrate and direct inside the play — 'you be the troll, I'm trip-trapping now'.
Children give each character its own voice and keep dialogue going back and forth between two puppets.
Children invent their own stories with characters and rules, and return to them across days.
Children sustain shared storytelling with friends — assigning roles, negotiating props, agreeing what happens next.
Quieter children contribute ideas through the puppet at group times, growing visibly in confidence.
Children name the puppet's feelings and suggest what would help it feel better.
Children draw on a wide repertoire of known stories, songs and rhymes to fuel their performances.

enhancements: A shadow-puppet screen and torch for retelling a core story in silhouette.
A puppet hospital — buttons, felt and a willing adult with a needle — so a loved puppet's ripped ear becomes a story of its own.
Blank wooden spoons, fabric scraps and wool for children to make the exact character their story needs.
A story stone bag: pull three stones (a key, a dog, a storm) and see what tale falls out.
A ticket table and row of chairs — children run the theatre: seats, tickets, 'quiet please', applause.
Record a child's puppet show and play it back — hearing their own story voice is powerful stuff.
A feelings puppet who visits group time with a real dilemma to solve — someone snatched, someone's left out.

playing_exploring: Children step into role and try out being someone — or something — else entirely.
The low stakes of 'the puppet said it' invite children to have a go who otherwise wouldn't.
active_learning: Children keep a performance going to its end, holding an audience and a storyline at once.
They rework the same story again and again, polishing the good bits.
creating_thinking: Children combine known stories into new ones — a wolf at the bears' cottage — and chase the consequences.
Choosing how a story ends, and defending that choice, is real decision-making.
